extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent drafters, inventors, and scholars of patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative standards for drafting patent claims: how claims must be written, what they may and may not cover, their relation to the specification/description, and doctrines (e.g., disclaimers, equivalents) that affect claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must definitely state what inventor intends to protect
rubrics_metrics.description: That what the inventor intends to protect must be definitely described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every claim must definitely state the invention the inventor intends to secure; modifications of the invention the inventor intends to protect must be definitely described (cases cited: Saigent v. Carter, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: If only part is claimed, the claim must show it
rubrics_metrics.description: That if the patentee intends to claim only a part of what he has described as essential to the invention the Claim must show it, or all will be considered as claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inventor describes several features but intends to claim only some, the claim must manifest that intent; otherwise the whole described subject-matter may be treated as claimed (cases: Evans v. Kelly; McMillin v. Rees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of adjunctive devices across claims
rubrics_metrics.description: That the adjunctive devices referred to in all the Claims for an invention must be the same in themselves and in their relation to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adjuncts are referenced across multiple claims, they should be consistent in identity and relationship; inconsistent or varying adjunct descriptions risk ambiguity or invalid claims (Ex parte Stanbridge cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumeration of elements as operative invention is proper
rubrics_metrics.description: That the enumeration of such elements as constitute the operative invention is a proper mode of claiming it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listing the constituent elements of a combination as the claimed invention is an acceptable way to define a combination claim (see Ex parte Farrow and related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not state elements not essential to the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That elements not essential to the invention should not be stated in the Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-essential or merely auxiliary elements should generally be omitted from claims; including them can obscure the real invention and create defects (see discussion on auxiliary elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must not include matter not embraced in intended invention
rubrics_metrics.description: That a Claim must not include any parts, features, or other matters not embraced in the invention intended to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be confined to the invention the patentee seeks to secure; inclusion of unrelated matter (Ex parte Skinner, Ex parte Wheat, Ex parte Wilber) is improper and can render a claim invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: When device useful only as part of a whole, other parts may be implied
rubrics_metrics.description: That when a device as claimed is useful only as part of a whole, the other parts will be understood as implied in the Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed device necessarily functions only with other unclaimed parts, courts may read those parts into the claim by implication (Ex parte West cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim auxiliary or merely auxiliary elements
rubrics_metrics.description: That what is described as merely auxiliary must not be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matter characterized in the specification as auxiliary, not essential, should not be elevated into the claim; doing so risks overreaching (Ex parte Wheat example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims covering useless things not void unless claimed as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: That a Claim covering useless things is not void unless they are claimed as essential to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of useless matter in a claim does not automatically void it unless the useless matter is asserted as essential to the claimed invention (case law examples cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: If invention is new only for certain purposes, claim must be limited to those purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the invention is new and patentable only when considered with reference to certain purposes or objects, it must be claimed only in connection with such purposes or objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim to an instrument or art that is old in itself but new in a particular use must specifically claim the new use or mode of operation; a claim to the old instrument without that limitation would be void (illustrated by new use doctrine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must distinguish from all known inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Claim must distinguish the art or instrument which it embraces from every art or instrument already known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must identify the novel features that separate the claimed subject-matter from the prior art; the claim should express no more and no less than necessary to convey an accurate understanding of the invention (Section §513 and cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim should be neither broader nor narrower than necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The Claim should express no more and no less than is necessary to convey an accurate understanding of the actual invention which had been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overbroad claims (claiming more than the inventor made) and underbroad claims (failing to capture the actual invention) are both problematic. If an additional independent feature is the essence of the invention, the claim should focus on that feature and stop there rather than enumerating unrelated old elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must avoid including matter previously patented or in public possession
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim including any matter before patented, or in possession of the public, is fatally defective; such matter should not be mentioned unless expressly disclaimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should not incorporate previously patented/public matter; if necessary, the applicant must disclaim the old subject-matter clearly. A disclaimer in a pending application must explain and not contradict the claim (cases and notes cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must set forth the invention in its most perfect concrete form (best mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Claim must set forth the invention it purports to describe in that form which, according to the judgment of the inventor, most perfectly embodies it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor is obliged to disclose the best mode in description and claim the concrete form best fitted for practical use. Once the best mode is described and claimed, other forms are presumptively embraced unless disclaimed (§514 and cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: A claim for making or doing covers all modes of making/doing it
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for the making of a thing or the doing of an act covers all modes of making or doing it, although only one mode is described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim properly describes the making/doing, it will be read to cover all practicable modes—not limited to the single example described (Union Paper Bag Mach. Co. v. Nixon, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim for a new shape covers other shapes expressing same idea
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for a new shape of an object covers all other shapes expressing the same idea of means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention is essentially a new idea expressed by a shape, variations that embody the same idea are protected (Winans v. Denmead examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must correspond with the description (no claim broader than described matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Claim is the request for protection and must entirely correspond with the Description and be based upon the matter therein contained; no invention can be claimed unless previously described so a skilled person could practice it without further inventive skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims cannot broaden beyond the disclosed description; features not delineated in the specification cannot be inserted into the claim even if a mechanic would discover them. A claim based on an insufficient description is void (numerous cases cited under §515).

rubrics_metrics.name: Description may illustrate the claim but may not enlarge it; claim controls when conflict exists
rubrics_metrics.description: The Claim may be illustrated but not enlarged by the Description; when the Description and Claim disagree, the Claim controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description cannot be used to expand the legal scope of a claim; where conflict makes the whole ambiguous, the invention must be found in one or the other and contradictions can render the whole void (McKesson v. Camdick; Railroad Co. v. Mellon examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter described as auxiliary not essential cannot be claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: Features of the invention described as auxiliary, but not essential to the invention, cannot be stated in the Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auxiliary matter that is not part of the inventive essence should not be claimed; claims should focus on essential elements (repeated principle across sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot claim all modes of effecting an end if only one mode described
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for all modes of effecting a result when the invention has been previously described as a single mode of effecting it is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot claim the entire genus of ways to achieve a result if the specification only describes a single specific mode; that would improperly broaden the claim (Lawther v. Hamilton; Ex parte Demming cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must not cover a mere principle or force of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: That the Claim must not cover a force of nature, a principle, or an abstract generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to abstract principles or natural forces are improper (Detmold v. Reeves; Ex parte Fairbanks; Burr v. Duryee examples). The claimable subject-matter must be a practical, operative application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims may be narrower than described; claim single operative element if sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention claimed may be narrower than that described; if a single new element in the described invention is a complete operative means it may be claimed alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A restricted claim to a single new operative element is permissible and can indirectly protect the whole invention if that element is essential to operation (Ex parte Sturges, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: No particular form of words required, but clarity and precision needed
rubrics_metrics.description: No particular form of words is required for the statement of the Claim; language must be sufficiently clear and accurate to define the invention to the mind of the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While formalistic phrasing is unnecessary, claims must convey the essential character of the invention precisely; general/ambiguous claims are void, though inartificial phrasing that does not create uncertainty is tolerated (§516 and case law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid useless words, multiplicity of synonyms, and equivocal terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Useless words should not be inserted nor synonymous words be multiplied; equivocal words are never permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superfluous or repetitive wording tends to create ambiguity; equivocal phrasing renders claims doubtful and can lead to invalidity (examples and case citations provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Every claimed element must be clearly stated, not merely inferred
rubrics_metrics.description: Every element claimed must be clearly stated, not merely inferred; a Claim must assert, not rest in doubtful implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely refer the reader to the description without asserting the invention are insufficient; vague or inferred elements are grounds for rejection (Ex parte Holt; Fricke v. Hum examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use indefinite expressions like 'means' or 'mechanism' without clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim cannot use such indefinite expressions as 'means,' 'mechanism,' etc., in a way that leaves essential elements undefined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words like 'means' or 'mechanism' may be used to denote non-essential appliances but cannot be used to obscure or omit essential elements of the invention; indefinite terminology that fails to disclose the invention is impermissible (Ex parte Holt, Ex parte Demming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalents are covered but should not be expressly claimed; use with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalents are legally covered by a Claim though not mentioned, but the term 'equivalent' or expressly claiming equivalents is equivocal and should be inhibited; 'or equivalent devices' must not be used unless equivalents are described or other special conditions apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine of equivalents operates to cover unanticipated equivalents, so expressly adding 'equivalents' may create undefined scope. Expressly claiming equivalents is generally improper unless the specification describes them or unless claiming one would completely bar claiming the other (cases: Burden v. Coming; Ex parte Reid; Ex parte Bogart; Ex parte Dolph).
